promptInstructions: Draft a Criminal Revision Petition under S.438 BNSS (calling for records; was S.397 CrPC) read with S.440 BNSS (Sessions Judge's powers of revision; was S.399 CrPC) or S.442 BNSS (High Court's powers of revision; was S.401 CrPC).

BNSS provisions: S.438 — the High Court or a Sessions Judge may call for and examine the record; S.440 — Sessions Judge's powers of revision; S.441 — powers of an Additional Sessions Judge; S.442 — High Court's powers of revision; S.443 — High Court's power to withdraw or transfer revision cases.
Note: S.438(2) BNSS — like S.397(2) CrPC — bar on revision against INTERLOCUTORY orders. Final / quasi-final orders only.
Test for interlocutory: orders that decide important rights or affect ends of trial are NOT interlocutory; orders of pure procedural nature ARE interlocutory.
Order of cognizance / summons is NOT interlocutory (revisable).
Bar of second revision under S.397(3) CrPC (now S.438(3) BNSS — bar to apply to both HC and Sessions in same case); HC can still exercise inherent jurisdiction.
REVISION IS SUPERVISORY, NOT APPELLATE. Scope: (i) correctness, (ii) legality, (iii) propriety of finding/sentence/order; or (iv) regularity of proceedings.
Revisional court has limited scope; cannot re-appreciate evidence like appellate court.
Perversity threshold for interference with factual findings in revision.

Grounds for revision: (a) jurisdictional error — court acted without jurisdiction or in excess; (b) illegality — order contrary to law or in disregard of mandatory procedure; (c) impropriety — order shocks conscience or breaches established norms; (d) factual perversity — only where finding is perverse, no evidence, or based on inadmissible evidence.
Para 1: Description of parties and status.
Para 2: Impugned order details — court, date, parties, case number.
Para 3: Brief factual background — proceedings below.
Para 4: Nature of impugned order — confirm it is NOT interlocutory.
Para 5: Limitation — Lawie prints this paragraph from the dates given; do not write it
Para 6: Whether appeal lay — where an appeal lies and none was brought, no revision at the instance of the party who could have appealed (S.442 BNSS; was S.401(4) CrPC); revision is residual.
Para 7: Whether earlier revision was filed — bar under S.438(3) BNSS — only one revision (to either HC or Sessions, not both).
Para 8: Grounds of revision — itemise each ground.
Para 9: Specific errors — paragraph-by-paragraph of impugned order with reasoning.
Para 10: Where lower court took cognizance / framed charge: cognizance / summoning orders, judicial mind required.
Para 11: Where Magistrate erred in framing charges: charge framing principles.
Para 12: Where lower court misapplied BNS / Special Act ingredients — section-by-section analysis.
Para 13: Where there is procedural irregularity prejudicing fair trial.
Para 14: Interim stay sought — typically of further proceedings in trial court.
Para 15: Documents relied on — certified copies of impugned order, chargesheet, witness statements, lower court order sheet.
Note: In revision, evidence cannot be re-appreciated as appellate court would. Findings of fact stand unless perverse.

Choice of forum: Where the impugned order is by a Magistrate — revision lies to the Sessions Judge (S.438 read with S.440 BNSS) or to the High Court (S.438 read with S.442 BNSS), not both (S.438(3) BNSS). Where the impugned order is by a Sessions Court — revision lies to the High Court. Strategic — Sessions revision may be quicker; the High Court also has inherent powers (S.528 BNSS).
Affidavit in support is mandatory.
Append Lawie disclaimer.
Do not name any judgment. Where an authority would normally be cited, write [Authority — add if relied upon].

key_citations: Madhu Limaye v. State of Maharashtra (1977) 4 SCC 551 — Interlocutory order definition
Amar Nath v. State of Haryana (1977) 4 SCC 137 — Interlocutory order test
Rajendra Kumar Sitaram Pande v. Uttam (1999) 3 SCC 134 — Cognizance order not interlocutory
Krishnan v. Krishnaveni (1997) 4 SCC 241 — Bar on second revision; HC's inherent jurisdiction
Kaptan Singh v. State of MP (2011) 6 SCC 705 — Revisional scope limited
State of Kerala v. Puttumana Illath Jathavedan Namboodiri (1999) 2 SCC 452 — Perversity threshold
Bhushan Kumar v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2012) 5 SCC 424 — Cognizance / summoning orders
Asim Shariff v. NIA (2019) 7 SCC 148 — Charge framing principles applied
State of Maharashtra v. Som Nath Thapa (1996) 4 SCC 659 — Charge framing standard
